SKOC42: Digital Marketing Communication 2026

Section 01: Defining Marketing Communication

Section One

Marketing Communication


  • Marketing defined: Identifying, anticipating & satisfying customer requirements profitably
  • Facilitates the ‘exchange of value’ between manufacturers and consumers
  • Strategic techniques for acquiring new customers (CRM)
  • Develops long-term customer relationships
  • Foundation for all digital marketing activity

B2C and B2B Models


  • Transaction types: B2C: organization sells directly to individual consumers
  • B2B: inter-organizational transactions between two or more businesses
  • B2B involves complex buying units and longer decision cycles
  • Different demand patterns: derived vs. direct consumer demand
  • Communication strategies differ significantly between models

D2C and C2B


  • Modern models: D2C: brands sell directly via digital media, bypassing intermediaries
  • C2B: consumers approach businesses with offers or feedback
  • Both reflect digital transformation of business models
  • D2C removes friction and shortens the path to purchase
  • C2B examples: freelance platforms, user reviews, crowdsourcing

C2C and User-Generated Content


  • Peer interactions: C2C: informational or financial exchanges between individuals
  • Mediated through third-party platforms (eBay, Airbnb, Reddit)
  • UGC includes reviews, comments, and social media posts
  • Peer recommendations are highly influential for new customers
  • Brand communities amplify trust and word-of-mouth

The AIDA Model


  • Classic hierarchy: Attention: create brand awareness, cut through clutter
  • Interest: arouse curiosity about product attributes
  • Desire: build affective preference and positive brand image
  • Action: trigger purchase or trial behavior
  • Assumes a linear ‘think–feel–do’ sequence

Marketing vs. Branding


  • Key distinction: Marketing manages customer requirements and commercial returns
  • Branding distinguishes a product by sum of perceived characteristics
  • Digital branding uses technology to create brand value
  • Brand image, personality, and reflection are core branding goals
  • Both disciplines operate together in integrated campaigns

Marketing vs. PR


  • Communication goals: Marketing focuses on facilitating competition and driving sales
  • PR manages awareness, understanding, and organizational reputation
  • PR targets ‘publics’ rather than customers alone
  • PR seen as ‘symmetrical’ but often fosters favorable evaluations
  • Integrated strategies align both for consistent messaging

Ethics in Marketing


  • Integrity vs. deception: Ethical marketing adheres to accepted moral standards
  • Misleading claims exploit pragmatic inferences — literally true, figuratively false
  • The ‘truth effect’: repeated claims feel credible due to familiarity
  • Regulators increasingly scrutinize digital advertising claims
  • Transparency builds long-term brand trust

Covert Persuasion


  • Hidden influence: Traditional marketing is an identified form of communication
  • Product placement: paid inclusion of brands in media content
  • Native advertising matches editorial design to appear organic
  • Influencer marketing blurs line between opinion and promotion
  • Disclosure regulations aim to protect consumer autonomy

AIDA Communication Objectives


  • Strategic alignment: Attention → Awareness objective: cut through advertising clutter
  • Interest/Desire → Persuasion: build preference and positive affect
  • Action → Behavior: convert preference into purchase
  • KPIs should map to each AIDA stage
  • Different channels suit different stages of the model

Section 02: Advertising Psychology

Section Two

Breaking Through Clutter


  • Attention: Attention: process by which a stimulus enters conscious awareness
  • Salience: contextual contrast makes an ad stand out
  • Vividness: emotional interest sustains engagement
  • Preattentive analysis: stimuli stored in implicit memory without focus
  • Advertisers must compete with ever-increasing media noise

Engaging the Consumer


  • Interest: Focal attention: stimulus is identified and categorized consciously
  • Arouses curiosity about product attributes and availability
  • Simple, comprehensible messages reduce miscomprehension
  • Historical miscomprehension rates of ads can exceed 30%
  • Storytelling and relevance drive sustained interest

Creating Brand Desire


  • Desire: Affective phase: thinking leads to emotional responses
  • Goal: create positive brand image by highlighting desirable attributes
  • Evaluative conditioning transfers positive affect from context to brand
  • Music, visuals, and endorsers shape emotional responses
  • Brand preference formed before purchase decision

Facilitating Purchase


  • Action: Conative/behavioral response: consumer purchases or tries the product
  • Purchase facilitation: ensuring ability and opportunity to act
  • For low-involvement products, ‘do’ may precede ‘think’ or ‘feel’
  • Frictionless checkout, availability, and pricing all matter
  • CTAs and landing page design critical for conversion

Dual Process Theories


  • ELM and HSM: Explain information processing based on motivation and ability
  • Systematic (central route): thorough evaluation of message arguments
  • Heuristic (peripheral route): simple rules like ‘experts know best’
  • High involvement → central route; low involvement → peripheral
  • Source attractiveness and credibility act as heuristic cues

Memory: Explicit vs. Implicit


  • Memory types: Explicit memory: conscious recollection, measured by recall & recognition
  • Implicit memory: prior exposure facilitates performance without awareness
  • Priming activates concepts that influence behavior unconsciously
  • Brand familiarity builds implicit preference over time
  • Repeated exposure increases fluency and perceived truth

Source Credibility


  • Trust and attraction: Credibility = expertise + trustworthiness
  • Most effective when processing motivation is low
  • Source attractiveness creates a ‘halo effect’ on product evaluations
  • Indirect sources: the brand itself; direct sources: spokespeople
  • Celebrity mismatch with product category reduces effectiveness

Message Strategies


  • Argument quality: Argument quality: persuasiveness of supporting claims
  • Two-sided ads admit minor negatives to increase honesty
  • Primacy effect: first arguments have strongest recall
  • Recency effect: last arguments recalled better after a delay
  • Strong arguments matter most under high involvement processing

Resistance to Persuasion


  • Reactance: Persuasion knowledge: consumer theories about advertiser motives
  • Psychological reactance: threat to freedom triggers ‘boomerang’ effect
  • High-pressure tactics backfire with informed consumers
  • Two-sided ads and product placement reduce resistance
  • Transparency and authenticity are antidotes to reactance

Digital Advertising Trust


  • The Google effect: Online trust driven by ability, benevolence, and integrity beliefs
  • The ‘Google effect’: Internet used as transactive external memory
  • Behavioral targeting uses past behavior to personalize ad messages
  • Privacy concerns erode trust when targeting is perceived as intrusive
  • Contextual advertising increasingly replaces cookie-based tracking

Section 03: Digital Marketing

Section Three

Analog vs. Digital Marketing


  • Push vs. pull: Analog media: push media — one-way broadcast to passive recipients
  • Digital marketing: pull media and inbound — consumers seek solutions
  • Digital is a ‘lean-forward’ medium demanding control and responsiveness
  • Interactivity, personalization, and real-time feedback are digital advantages
  • Multichannel strategies integrate both analog and digital touchpoints

Web 1.0: The Informational Web


  • Brochureware era: Characterized by static 'brochureware' sites with limited interaction
  • Replicated offline marketing literature in a one-to-many format
  • Personal homepages: text-heavy, functioning as digital résumés
  • No user-generated content; webmaster controlled all publishing
  • Communication was one-directional — brand to consumer only

Web 2.0: The Participatory Web


  • Social era: Defined by social networking and user-generated content
  • Consumer role shifts from passive recipient to ‘co-constructor’
  • eWOM and earned media more strategically important than paid
  • Platforms: YouTube, Facebook, Wikipedia, blogs, forums
  • Brands must participate in conversations, not just broadcast

Web 3.0: The Intelligent Web


  • AI and personalization: High levels of micro-customization across all devices
  • AI enables predictive modeling and personalized messaging
  • Semantic web: machines understand context and meaning
  • 5G, VR, and AR enable immersive consumer experiences
  • Automated and always-on marketing at scale

Digital Marketing Channels


  • Six categories: Search Engine Marketing: SEO and paid search (PPC)
  • Social Media Marketing: organic and paid social campaigns
  • Display Advertising: banners, video pre-rolls, programmatic
  • Digital PR: influencer outreach, mentions, and editorial links
  • Digital Messaging: email newsletters and mobile push notifications

The FAMGA Ecosystem


  • Platform dominance: FAMGA: Facebook, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Apple
  • These platforms mediate interactions via proprietary infrastructure
  • Each has unique algorithms governing search and social reach
  • Data ownership by platforms limits marketer transparency
  • Walled gardens require platform-specific strategies

The RACE Framework


  • Digital analytics: Reach: build awareness — impressions, traffic, social reach
  • Act: encourage site interaction — pages/visit, lead generation
  • Convert: achieve sales — conversion rate, revenue, AOV
  • Engage: build loyalty — NPS, repeat purchase, CLV
  • Clickstream analysis maps the full visitor path to optimize conversion

VQVC Metrics


  • SMART objectives: Volume: unique visitors, sessions, and ad impressions
  • Quality: conversion rates, bounce rates, time on page
  • Value: ROI, goal value, average order value (AOV)
  • Cost: CPC, CPA, and overall media efficiency ratios
  • SMART targets defined for each VQVC dimension per channel

Customer Satisfaction Online


  • Voice of the customer: Online experience: rational and emotional factors shape perceptions
  • Service-quality gap identified through VoC feedback tools
  • Net Promoter Score (NPS) measures advocacy and loyalty
  • Repeat purchase intention as key satisfaction indicator
  • User testing and heatmaps reveal experience friction points

Conversion Optimization


  • CRO and AB testing: CRO: structured experiments to improve site effectiveness
  • AB testing compares page versions to identify higher performers
  • Multivariate tests assess combinations of page elements simultaneously
  • Continuous cycle: diagnose → hypothesize → test → optimize
  • Small CRO gains compound significantly at scale

Section 04: SOSTAC Planning Framework

Section Four

Situation Analysis


  • Digital SWOT: Audit the digital marketplace: SWOT and competitor benchmarking
  • Map competitor capabilities across the RACE framework
  • Low-involvement: focus on visibility and simple triggers
  • High-involvement: map complex path-to-purchase across touchpoints
  • Customer persona research grounds the analysis in real behavior

Setting Objectives


  • SMART goals: Set numerical targets for business contribution (% online sales)
  • Define marketing outcomes: leads, engagement, brand recall
  • Low-involvement: prioritize Volume (reach and frequency)
  • High-involvement: prioritize Quality (leads) and Value (depth)
  • Objectives must be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound

Strategy and STP


  • Targeting: Define the Online Value Proposition (OVP) clearly
  • Select target segments and build detailed customer personas
  • Low-involvement: affect-based creative appeals
  • High-involvement: argument-based appeals supporting think–feel–do
  • Positioning determines how brand is perceived vs. competitors

Tactics: The Digital Mix


  • 7Ps applied: Select optimal mix across the six digital media channels
  • Apply 7Ps: Product, Price, Place, Promotion, People, Process, Physical
  • Low-involvement: push media such as display ads and video
  • High-involvement: pull media (SEO, content) for proactive research
  • Channel selection driven by audience behavior and budget allocation

Campaign Execution


  • Action planning: Develop campaign timeline and editorial content calendar
  • Manage multichannel communications across paid, owned, earned
  • Low-involvement: seasonal ‘burst’ campaigns and real-time marketing
  • High-involvement: always-on lifecycle communications
  • Agile iteration: review results weekly and adapt creative

Performance Control


  • Analytics and optimization: Use digital dashboards to track KPIs against SMART targets
  • Conduct AB testing continuously to optimize conversion
  • Low-involvement control: reach and frequency metrics
  • High-involvement control: attribution modeling for complex journeys
  • Regular reporting cadence closes the feedback loop
